title: C++26 Disapproved (andreasfertig.com)
comments: As someone who writes high-reliability C++ but is completely outside the standards process, I see the issues with C++ Contracts. It isn’t clear that it solves a problem that anyone has in real codebases, especially after C++20 concepts.If you were already writing high-reliability C++ then the benefits are difficult to quantify. If you weren’t writing high-reliability C++ then it saves you almost nothing over doing the standard idioms of high-reliability C++ that were already available to you at very marginally more cost. It does standardize expression of it in narrow cases but the payoff seems minimal.Most of what C++ Contracts delivers is a mashup of what you can already do with constexpr and C++20 Concepts. I like reliability features but this feature, as delivered, looks fairly useless if you already use reliability features. A compelling standard would need to make much deeper guarantees out of the box. And the compiler can already see through most compositions of constexpr and C++20 concepts, which is already very expressive.C++ Contracts looks a bit like a feature that was designed long before current standard features existed.reply
Your comment just made me realize contracts is different from concepts (which are basically bounded genetics, right…?)reply

C++ concepts evaluate the properties of types at compile-time. You can inject arbitrary constraints on type properties anywhere in the code including conditional codegen. It is a way of asking if a type “can express this complex set of abstract things or has this enumerated set of properties” with almost arbitrary detail. They are extremely powerful in terms of expressiveness and specialization of code. Insanely good for performance and reliability engineering.One of the best features to be added to C++ in many years.C++ contracts are an attempt to bring C asserts into the C++ age. The weakness of C++ contracts is that they are mostly syntactic sugar over C asserts. If you really care about this type of thing, you probably already have a custom C++ assertion framework that is at least as nuanced if not more.The promise of C++ contracts is that they can aid formal verification, which would be great. As delivered, it can’t do much more than was already possible, which will inhibit adoption.reply

The weakness of C++ contracts is that they are mostly syntactic sugar over C asserts. 

The sugar is actually one of my issues with them. The evaluation semantics are much more complicated / potentially slower than C asserts because of the sugar, and why you would have to pay those costs isn't obvious at first glance. Lisa Lippincott's excellent talk on the design of contracts [0] is what switched me from a sort of neutral support to disliking it. I think it's a stupid place for the national bodies to draw the line though. std::regex is acceptable, but a nothingburger like contracts tanks the vote?[0] https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yhhSW-FSWkEreply

To be clear, I have a lot of issues with the contracts proposal. I probably wouldn’t use despite living out on the standards frontier. I don’t even use C asserts already because they are not expressive enough in important ways. This proposal kind of reifies the inadequacies.I think the risk is that C++ contracts become an evolutionary dead-end that hang around forever in code bases because they were standardized. It wouldn’t be the first time this has happened.reply
A concept is a compile time requirement that bounds templates which are the generics in C++, so you are close.reply

Concepts are evaluated compile time and make a lot of TMP more elegant. Contracts are runtime check, akin to assertions.Phrased differently, contracts are to concepts what assert is to static_assert.reply
Concepts are for Types at compile time while Contracts are for Values at runtime.reply
Huh? Concepts are types of types. Contracts are fancier, structured runtime assertions. What does one have to do with the other? They're nothing alike.reply
They both start with the letter C, have two syllables, and have/had a hard time getting into the standard.  If you’re not paying close attention, it’s easy to get them confused.reply

Chapter 12 (full-text search) quietly changed under this book in Postgres 18: FTS now reads its dictionaries and config through the cluster's default collation provider instead of always libc, so clusters on ICU or the new builtin PG_UNICODE_FAST can see different behavior in FTS and pg_trgm — the release notes explicitly tell you to reindex those indexes after pg_upgrade. Also in 18, LIKE with nondeterministic collations stopped being an error, which was the main reason people avoided case-insensitive ICU collations on searchable columns.reply

The HOT chapter is the one with the most direct practical payoff. Two things worth knowing from it: HOT only kicks in when no indexed column changes and the new tuple fits on the same page, so an index on a frequently-updated column (status, updated_at) quietly disables it for every update to that table. And lowering fillfactor (say 80-90) on update-heavy tables leaves free space on each page so HOT can actually happen. Comparing n_tup_hot_upd to n_tup_upd in pg_stat_user_tables is a cheap way to see whether you're getting HOT updates before tuning anything.reply
Depends on how wide your columns are and how often your records are modified. Past a certain width and I’m not sure lowering fillfactor is a good idea.reply

I started using an "engineering notebook" for things like that. They are called other things in other lines of work or school (lab notebook, captain's log, ...). In an actual engineering notebook, you would use a sewn binding where you can't add or remove pages, the pages are numbered, you have an index in the front, entries are made in strictly chronological order, you'd have someone else witness and sign pages, draw a diagonal line across empty areas so you can't remove things, only cross things out with a single line, etc. All that because you might need to prove you invented something and other legal CYA reasons. Most of these requirements, you don't need for personal projects, though. But the things that are useful: keeping track of projects, what settings you've tried, what the results were, and so on. That way you don't have to reproduce it from scratch again later. "What settings did I need use to create the gerber files in kicad for manufacturing? How did I set ___ in the oscilloscope? What parts did I use to make that thing? What things did I wish I had checked last time? Where did I put those files?" You can also print things out and tape them in for reference.reply

title: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand (arstechnica.com)
comments: Anyone that's never had the (dis)pleasure of working with tapes, there's some gotchas to know about before archiving and forgetting about it.When you create an archive, do not skip the step of reading it back. I'm not talking about just having the system confirm it is readable. I mean actually restoring the data from the tape. I've had tapes fail to retrieve data off of the tape even though the writing app confirmed it was readable.Drives can have issues reading data written by another drive. Drives can have issues reading a tape it wrote itself.Why write one when you can write two at twice the time/cost? In all of my experience with tape, I've never written just one tape. In the early days of DVDs, the images were written to LTO to send to have the discs pressed. Two were always sent on the chance one wasn't readable and schedules were so tight that the loss of a couple of days to send a new tape would wreck delivery dates. Another facility wrote three tapes: one kept on site, one sent to IronMountain, one sent to the client directly. Plenty of occasions saw the local copy unreadable and the IronMountain copy was retrieved. These were managed by large robotic tape libraries so each tape was written in a different drive at the same time so it was 3x cost while only 1x time.Use the drive cleaning cassette as recommended. Your dirty heads can cause the data to not be written/read correctly depending on which head is dirty. If you're having issues reading, clean the heads before giving up on the tape. If you're having issues reading a tape just written, do not think someone else will be able to read it.Ensure whoever might be using a tape you've written understands what was used to write the tape. Not all archivers are compatible. If you use the tar command to write to tape, people using a GUI app won't be able to read it.reply

I have worked with 5 different LTO tapes versions, 5 different other cassette formats (DAT, DDS, etc), and open spools… never, ever, ever in the 15 years had ANY problem (I’ve probably used 1000 of them). We did cycle them very often, we did have proper maintenance of the drives, through. Now that, compared with RAID Disk arrays, where we had monthly failures, was much better. Also I would not trust the „semi-permanent“ NVMEs, where after 1 year without power they get basically resetreply
1000 is a lot but it sounds like GP was a few orders of magnitude higher.reply

Yeah, we'd do 1000 in a year easy, but that number is easy to grow when every write takes 3 tapes. We had 3 robot towers each with 10 drives in them in our facility, and there were others at other facilities. There was an entire department for interacting with them. If the tape with your data was in a robot, you could have the restore started within an hour. If the tape was in the onsite library, it would be within a few hours as they decided what tape to unload from a robot.reply
I worked with a few more orders of magnitude and saw lots of errors.reply
What order of magnitude were the errors compared to the number of tapes?  1%?  0.1%?  0.01%?reply
If the error is 1 in 1,000 it's likely never to be found.  How often is data retrieved from tape?reply
If you follow the advice to have it read immediately after written, then 100% of tapes have data retrieved.reply

When I hear wildly differing stories like this I often wonder how much environmental conditions play a factor in the different experiences that people have.Perhaps one of you is living in a much more humid and/or hot environment that causes issues with the writing process.reply

Tapes were constantly kept in the data center, so constant temperature and humidity 25C/50%. As I said, Tapes were changed after N uses, drives properly serviced. So if you leave them at home, in the sun in summer and in winter expose them to 10C with humidity from 10% to 90%, old drives, never clean heads… IdK
That all being said, when I started working there, in my ignorance, I said “TAPES?!?! They are not reliable” due to my experience with audio tapes. But I was laughed at, and they told me about people putting 10 9 track spools in a car [0] (by the way, the same we used for billing backups!) and they went literally thousands of miles driving on partially dirt roads, in summer w/o AC, doing updates to systems, and also never ever had an issue. They were so sure they would work, that they did not take a second set, even when driving 1000 miles, and a read error would mean going back!!![0] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9-track_tapereply

first_paragraph: 3rd November 2026Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. For the last 50 or so years, humanity has been busily creating and digitizing an enormous public record of human knowledge. Most obviously, Wikipedia’s editors have assembled the most comprehensive encyclopedia humanity has ever produced. A vigorous open source movement created a couple petabytes of software source code. Communities on Stack Exchange spent more than a decade asking questions, arguing about answers, and carefully curating the results. Scientists uploaded their papers to ArXiv. Project Gutenberg—almost as old as the internet itself—produced digital editions of out-of-copyright books.And of course, billions of people made websites, commented, had arguments both petty and profound, uploaded photos and paintings, wrote fiction, and—believe it or not—sometimes went and told lies on the internet.
